Executive Summary and the 2025–2026 Legislative Paradigm Shift

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program stands as the federal government's single largest fiscal mechanism supporting industrial innovation, technological advancement, and experimental engineering. Administered operationally by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) while fiscal and legislative policy parameters are established by the Department of Finance Canada, the program operates through a dual-pillar statutory architecture under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.). The first pillar permits an immediate or indefinitely carryforwardable deduction of qualifying SR&ED expenditures against business income under Section 37 of the Act, overriding general prohibitions against capital and pre-production deductions. The second pillar generates refundable and non-refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Act. When stacked with provincial and territorial research and development incentives—most notably in Québec, Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, and the Atlantic provinces—the Canadian fiscal regime reduces the net after-tax cost of qualifying research and development expenditures more aggressively than almost any other Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) jurisdiction.

Between 2012 and 2024, federal legislative amendments progressively narrowed the qualifying SR&ED expenditure base. During that twelve-year contractionary cycle, Parliament reduced the basic federal ITC rate from 20% to 15% for taxation years ending after 2013, restricted the eligibility of arm's-length subcontractor payments and third-party payments to 80% after 2012, lowered the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary overhead factor to 55%, and completely eliminated capital expenditures and Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) from SR&ED eligibility for depreciable property acquired after 2013 and before December 16, 2024. Those measures forced capital-intensive manufacturing, cleantech, hardware, and biotechnology enterprises to rely exclusively on regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation schedules rather than immediate SR&ED pooling and tax credits.

In a historic policy reversal introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the 2025 Federal Budget, and formally enacted into law through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal government executed the largest structural expansion of the SR&ED program in decades. Applying retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—and specifically to depreciable capital property acquired and becoming available for use, or equipment lease costs incurred, after December 15, 2024—Bill C-15 fundamentally reshapes corporate R&D tax planning across five interconnected structural dimensions.

First, Parliament doubled the maximum annual qualified expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% federal ITC rate from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, enabling qualifying corporations to earn up to $2,100,000 annually in enhanced federal ITCs before dropping down to the 15% basic credit rate. Second, for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out corridor has been widened from the legacy $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 bracket to a substantially broader range of $15,000,000 to $75,000,000, preserving the enhanced 35% refundable credit for mid-market domestic scale-ups. Third, for the first time in the modern history of the Income Tax Act, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) gain statutory access to the enhanced 35% ITC rate—with 100% cash refundability on current expenditures and 40% cash refundability on capital expenditures—on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures, subject to a gradual phase-out based on average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years. Crucially, CCPCs may also elect on an annual basis to utilize this three-year average gross revenue phase-out formula whenever it yields a higher federal expenditure limit than the traditional taxable capital calculation.

Fourth, Bill C-15 reinstates the eligibility of capital expenditures and Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024. Property intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more of its operating time or value) in SR&ED carried on in Canada once again qualifies for both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and SR&ED ITCs, attracting a 40% cash refundability rate on capital ITCs earned within the expenditure limit. Simultaneously, new machinery and equipment used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of operating time) in SR&ED in Canada qualifies under restored First Term and Second Term Shared-Use-Equipment rules at 25% of capital cost per term, alongside reinstated equipment lease cost eligibility. Fifth, as an administrative measure introduced in Budget 2025, the CRA launched, effective April 1, 2026, a formal Pre-Claim Approval Process accessible through My Business Account, allowing eligible businesses to obtain an upfront technical eligibility determination from the CRA within eight weeks prior to commencing R&D work or incurring project costs.

At the provincial level, parallel structural reforms have altered regional R&D tax planning, highlighted by Québec's 2025–2026 Budget consolidation of its fragmented legacy R&D tax credits into the unified Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC — crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation, also designated the Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Simultaneously, recent jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada—including Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108), Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159), Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63), and Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173)—has clarified the evidentiary thresholds governing hypothesis formulation, failed experimentation, oral testimony, and statute-barred reassessments.
Statutory Architecture and Federal Legislative Framework
Core Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The legal authority governing federal SR&ED incentives resides within a tightly integrated network of provisions in the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Unlike discretionary government grants or contribution programs, SR&ED tax incentives operate as statutory entitlements: any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that satisfies the technical definition of SR&ED, incurs qualified expenditures, and files prescribed forms within the statutory reporting window is legally entitled to both the income deduction and the investment tax credit.

body.text: The statutory interplay between Section 37 and Section 127 requires precise synchronization across consecutive taxation years. When a taxpayer claims an SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(5)—either to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable or to receive a cash refund under Section 127.1—the exact dollar amount of the federal ITC claimed in a given taxation year reduces the claimant's Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Income Tax Act. If the claimant has already deducted the entirety of its Section 37 expenditure pool in the prior year, the prior-year federal ITC claimed generates a negative pool adjustment at the end of the following year, which must be included directly in taxable business income under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the Act. Conversely, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits—such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), or Québec's CRIC—constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(18). Consequently, provincial tax credits reduce both the Section 37 deductible pool and the federal qualified expenditure base in the current taxation year in which those provincial credits are earned and receivable, unless the taxpayer formally renounces or waives the provincial credit on or before the filing-due date of its income tax return.
The Five-Criteria Technological Eligibility Framework

Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory architecture stratifies eligible core scientific or technological work into three foundational pillars, supplemented by an exhaustive fourth category of directly commensurate support activities. Under paragraph 248(1)(a), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph 248(1)(b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph 248(1)(c), experimental development—which accounts for over 90% of industrial SR&ED claims filed in Canada—encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Once a valid core project is established under paragraph (a), (b), or (c), paragraph 248(1)(d) permits the inclusion of support work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the Income Tax Act explicitly exclude routine commercial, extractive, and non-technological activities from SR&ED eligibility, even when performed by highly credentialled engineers or scientists. These statutory exclusions bar claims for market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.

In administering subsection 248(1), the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives harmonize the statutory definition with the binding five-question judicial test formulated by Justice Donald Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 TCC) and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393). As confirmed by the CRA's administrative history, both the agency's two-requirement framework—evaluating why the work was conducted (to achieve a scientific or technological advancement) and how the work was conducted (as a systematic investigation or search)—and the five Northwest Hydraulic questions are derived directly from the statutory text of subsection 248(1), providing a common legal vocabulary for claimants and CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs).

To substantiate technological eligibility during a CRA technical review, a claimant must first demonstrate the existence of a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty. Technological uncertainty arises where a system-level constraint, capability limitation, or fundamental gap in the underlying scientific or technological knowledge base prevents a competent professional in the field from predicting whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, using standard procedures, publicly available knowledge, or routine engineering. Purely commercial, financial, or scheduling uncertainties do not constitute technological uncertainty, although physical, chemical, or computational resource limits—such as memory footprint ceilings, thermal dissipation boundaries, network latency constraints, or microbial shelf-life instability—frequently create genuine system-level technological uncertainty.

Second, the claimant must formulate explicit hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the claimant must execute a systematic investigation or search following the scientific method, designing experiments or mathematical and computational models, isolating variables, observing and measuring quantitative results, and iteratively modifying hypotheses based on empirical analysis. The CRA explicitly cautions in its updated Form T661 instructions that if a study's end results cannot be measured or counted, the work may not be recognized as SR&ED. Fourth, the investigation must seek to yield a scientific or technological advancement that expands the technological knowledge base available to competent professionals in the field. Crucially, as affirmed by the Tax Court of Canada in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108), achieving commercial product targets is not required: the conclusive rejection of a hypothesis or the systematic elimination of unsuccessful formulations after structured analysis of why they failed constitutes a valid technological advancement. Fifth, the taxpayer must maintain contemporaneous records tracking the hypotheses formulated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained as the work progressed.

Within the software development, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, cybersecurity, and health technology sectors—which remain primary focal points of CRA compliance audits—routine software development is strictly delineated from qualifying experimental development. Configuring off-the-shelf application programming interfaces (APIs), porting legacy code across standard frameworks, resolving syntax bugs, or training established neural network architectures on clean datasets constitutes ineligible routine engineering. Conversely, software engineering qualifies as experimental development where engineers confront underlying architectural, algorithmic, scalability, concurrency, or cryptographic bottlenecks that cannot be resolved via standard documentation or routine debugging, necessitating formal hypothesis formulation, algorithmic redesign, controlled benchmarking, and quantitative performance analysis.
Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability Mechanics
Basic and Enhanced ITC Rate Structures

Under Section 127 of the Income Tax Act, as detailed in the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (revised October 7, 2026 to incorporate the legislative amendments announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the 2025 Federal Budget, and enacted via Bill C-15), federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits operate on a two-tier statutory rate structure. The basic federal ITC rate is 15% of a claimant's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year, calculated on the excess of that pool over any provincial super-allowance benefit amounts. This 15% basic rate applies universally to large corporations, foreign-controlled corporations, non-qualifying public corporations, individuals, trusts, members of partnerships, and to the qualified SR&ED expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit.

Above the 15% basic tier, subsection 127(10.1) provides an additional 20% credit enhancement, bringing the combined enhanced federal ITC rate to 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, eligibility for the 35% enhanced rate was restricted exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) throughout the taxation year, subject to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 transforms this structure in two ways: first, it extends the 35% enhanced ITC rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs); and second, it doubles the maximum annual expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for both CCPCs and ECPCs. Associated CCPCs must share and allocate this $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit among members of the associated corporate group by filing T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, revised May 29, 2026).
Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas and Revenue Election

The $6,000,000 maximum annual expenditure limit is governed by statutory phase-out formulas designed to concentrate the 35% enhanced refundable credit on small and medium-sized private enterprises and mid-market Canadian public innovators. Under the Bill C-15 rules effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Income Tax Act provides two distinct phase-out methodologies, granting CCPCs a valuable annual tax-planning election.

Under the first methodology, applicable by default to CCPCs, the expenditure limit phases out linearly based on the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporate group. Whereas the legacy rules for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024 phased out the $3,000,000 limit between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital, the post-December 15, 2024 formula begins reducing the $6,000,000 expenditure limit only when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, eliminating the limit entirely at $75,000,000. Expressed mathematically, for a CCPC using the taxable capital method in a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, the annual Expenditure Limit is determined as follows:

Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. Once prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches or exceeds $75,000,000, A equals $60,000,000 and the expenditure limit is reduced to nil, restricting the corporation to the 15% non-refundable basic ITC.

Under the second methodology, applicable to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is gradually reduced based on the average annual gross revenue of the corporation (and its consolidated corporate group) over the three preceding fiscal years, phasing out over the same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 corridor. Crucially, as confirmed by the CRA's October 7, 2026 SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, a CCPC may elect on a year-by-year basis using the prescribed form to calculate its federal expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average gross revenue method rather than prior-year taxable capital whenever the revenue method results in a higher expenditure limit. This annual election resolves a long-standing structural penalty faced by capital-intensive Canadian startups—such as biotechnology, semiconductor, aerospace, and clean-energy companies—that raise large rounds of equity or venture debt (pushing their balance-sheet taxable capital above $15,000,000 or $75,000,000) while remaining in pre-revenue or early commercialization stages.

In addition to the Expenditure Limit (which determines how much expenditure earns 35% versus 15%), Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act utilizes a separate threshold—the Qualifying Income Limit (QIL)—to determine whether a CCPC qualifies as a "qualifying corporation" eligible for 100% cash refundability on its 35% current ITCs and 40% cash refundability on its 15% ITCs above the expenditure limit. A qualifying corporation is a CCPC (alone or associated) whose taxable income in the previous taxation year (before considering specified future tax consequences) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit formula was:

Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is less than or equal to $10,000,000, and otherwise is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount of prior-year taxable capital exceeding $10,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 expands the Qualifying Income Limit formula to align with the widened $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital corridor:

Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada does not exceed $15,000,000, and otherwise is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount of prior-year taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000.
Comprehensive Federal ITC Rate and Refundability Matrix

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (October 7, 2026), the statutory ITC earning rate and the Section 127.1 cash refundability percentage depend on both the legal status of the claimant and whether the underlying qualified expenditures are current expenditures or capital expenditures (reinstated after December 15, 2024). Within the CCPC category, the Income Tax Act distinguishes between a "qualifying corporation" (whose prior-year taxable income did not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit) and an "excluded corporation" (a corporation that, at any time in the year, is controlled by, or related to, one or more persons exempt from tax under section 149, a province, a Canadian municipality or other public authority, or any combination of these); a CCPC that is neither—because its prior-year taxable income exceeded its Qualifying Income Limit—falls into a third category.

body.text: Several critical operational rules govern the application, allocation, and carryforward of these credits. First, even for a Qualifying CCPC or an ECPC that enjoys 100% cash refundability on the 35% ITC earned on current SR&ED expenditures up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, ITCs earned on qualified capital SR&ED expenditures (depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024) are refundable at 40%. The remaining 60% of the capital ITC is non-refundable and may be applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable for the year or carried back and forward. Second, any unused non-refundable federal SR&ED ITCs may be carried back up to 3 taxation years to recover Part I tax paid in prior years, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset future Part I corporate or personal income tax liabilities.

Third, specialized flow-through rules govern partnerships and trusts. Because a partnership is not a separate taxable entity under the Income Tax Act, SR&ED expenditures are incurred and calculated at the partnership level (supported by a separate Form T661 filed for each partnership), and each partner's reasonable share of the 15% SR&ED ITC from the partnership is allocated and added to the partner's own ITC pool for the taxation year. Corporate partners claim their allocated ITC on T2 Schedule 31, while individual partners claim their allocated ITC on Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)), receiving 40% cash refundability on unused credits. For trusts, a beneficiary's reasonably designated portion of an SR&ED ITC is added to the beneficiary's ITC calculation; however, under the amended trust rules in the Income Tax Act, only graduated rate estates and communal organizations deemed to be inter vivos trusts are legally permitted to designate SR&ED ITCs out to beneficiaries.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
Proxy Method Versus Traditional Method Election

When preparing an SR&ED claim, a taxpayer must formally elect in Part 1 of Form T661—by checking Field 160 for the Proxy Method or Field 162 for the Traditional Method—which accounting methodology it will use to calculate SR&ED overhead and other expenditures for the taxation year. Once Form T661 is filed with the CRA for a given taxation year, the election between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method is irrevocable for that taxation year, although the claimant remains free to switch methods in subsequent taxation years.

body.text: Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not track or include any actual SR&ED overhead or indirect expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional overhead amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661 pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, equal to 55% of the portion of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada. Because the PPA is a notional calculation rather than an actual cash outlay, it is not added to the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (as the underlying rent, utilities, and administrative overheads are already deductible under Section 9 of the Income Tax Act), but it is added directly to Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661 to earn federal and provincial Investment Tax Credits.

In computing the 55% PPA in Part 5, strict statutory exclusions and caps apply to the eligible salary base. Taxable employment benefits under Sections 6 and 7 of the Income Tax Act (such as stock options or automobile benefits), bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and deemed expenditures must be stripped out of the PPA salary base before multiplying by 55%. Furthermore, for any "specified employee"—defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation—the maximum annual salary eligible to enter the Part 5 PPA calculation is capped at 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined for purposes of the Canada Pension Plan (for instance, when the YMPE was updated to $61,600 for the 2021 calendar year, the maximum specified employee proxy salary base was $154,000, pro-rated by the number of days in the taxation year in which the individual was employed). Additionally, subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations imposes an overall ceiling ensuring that the total PPA claimed cannot exceed the taxpayer's total business deductions for the year net of specified statutory deductions.
Salaries, Wages, Materials, and Subcontractor Rules
Salaries and Wages of Employees

Salaries and wages incurred for employees performing SR&ED carried on in Canada—alongside permissible foreign SR&ED salaries incurred outside Canada up to a maximum of 10% of domestic direct SR&ED salaries under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)—constitute the primary expenditure driver of most Canadian SR&ED claims. For regular arm's-length employees, 100% of the portion of gross salaries, wages, vacation pay, statutory employer payroll contributions (Canada Pension Plan, Québec Pension Plan, Employment Insurance, provincial Employer Health Tax, and Workers' Compensation Board or CNESST assessments), and performance bonuses directly attributable to hands-on technical experimentation, commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d), or direct first-line technical supervision qualifies for both Section 37 deduction and Section 127 ITCs.

For specified employees (10% or greater shareholders and non-arm's-length employees), statutory anti-avoidance rules impose three strict constraints on Line 305/307 salary claims: first, bonuses and remuneration based on profits are completely disallowed; second, maximum directly engaged SR&ED salary claimable on Form T661 is capped at 5 times the YMPE (pro-rated for partial years); and third, specified employees may only claim time spent directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED or direct technical supervision, and are barred from claiming indirect administrative or clerical support tasks under the Traditional Method. Furthermore, under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any salary, wage, or bonus accrued at fiscal year-end that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year, must be excluded on Line 315 of Form T661, and may only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid.
Materials Consumed or Transformed

Claimants may include on Form T661 the cost of physical materials that are either consumed (rendered virtually valueless or destroyed during experimental trials) or transformed (physically integrated into an experimental prototype, custom test rig, or pilot plant) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Supplies that are not physically integrated into the experimental output or consumed directly in the experimental process do not qualify as materials, though they may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method (Line 360) or be covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method. If an experimental prototype or transformed material is subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED cost of the materials incorporated into that unit becomes subject to ITC and Section 37 pool recapture up to the lesser of the original material cost claimed and the proceeds of disposition or fair market value at the time of commercial conversion.
Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Non-Arm's-Length Transactions

The statutory treatment of outsourced research and supply transactions depends on whether the counterparty deals at arm's length with the claimant and whether the counterparty is a taxable Canadian supplier. Where a claimant engages an arm's-length contractor to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, but subsection 127(9) imposes a mandatory 20% reduction when computing qualified SR&ED expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661, such that only 80% of arm's-length SR&ED contract payments qualify to earn federal ITCs. Arm's-length contractor fees do not attract the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. Similarly, third-party payments made to approved Canadian universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D corporations for SR&ED carried on in Canada (where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results in its business) must be reported on a separate Schedule A (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) attached to Form T661 and are likewise subject to the 20% reduction (80% ITC inclusion).

By contrast, where SR&ED is performed on behalf of a claimant by a non-arm's-length (NAL) party, the contract payments made by the payer do not qualify as SR&ED expenditures for the payer, nor are they treated as contract payments reducing the performer's SR&ED pool. Instead, the NAL performer claims the underlying SR&ED salaries, materials, and overheads directly, or the two related parties may jointly execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, revised May 15, 2026) to transfer qualified SR&ED expenditures from the NAL performer to the NAL payer. As clarified in Appendix A.2 (Example 1) of the CRA's updated Total Qualified Expenditure Policy (May 22, 2026), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is included in the performer's total qualified SR&ED expenditures when determining the maximum transferable amount on Form T1146. On Form T661, the transferor reports the transferred amount on Line 540/544/546, while the transferee includes the transferred amount on Line 508/538.

When a claimant purchases goods or non-SR&ED services—or, after December 15, 2024, acquires or leases depreciable property—from a non-arm's-length supplier for use in SR&ED, subsections 127(11.6) and 127(11.7) of the Income Tax Act cap the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes at the NAL supplier's "adjusted selling cost" or "adjusted service cost," stripping out intercompany markups. The difference between the contract price and the NAL supplier's adjusted cost must be deducted as an adjustment on Line 543 of Form T661. Furthermore, under Section 9.0 of the CRA's Total Qualified Expenditure Policy (May 22, 2026), amounts paid or payable for an SR&ED contract to a non-taxable supplier (an entity exempt from Part I tax) must be deducted when computing qualified expenditures, because the non-taxable supplier is not subject to the deemed contract payment clawback under subsection 127(25). Similarly, Section 11.1 of the policy and paragraph (l) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act clarify that SR&ED expenditures incurred by a Crown-owned corporation—except for a Prescribed Federal Crown Corporation listed in Section 7100 of the Income Tax Regulations—are excluded from earning ITCs because the income of such Crown corporations is exempt from tax under subsection 149(1).
Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use-Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

One of the most consequential legislative reforms enacted through Bill C-15—and thoroughly codified in the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026)—is the full reinstatement of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs for property acquired or lease expenses incurred after December 15, 2024. Depreciable property acquired before December 16, 2024 remains strictly excluded from SR&ED tax incentives.
Full SR&ED Capital Expenditures and the All or Substantially All (ASA) Intent Tests

To claim 100% of the capital cost of depreciable property on Line 390 of Form T661—where capital cost encompasses the purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and other direct acquisition costs—the property must be acquired and become available for use after December 15, 2024, and the claimant must satisfy one of two statutory intent tests at the time of acquisition. Under the first test (the Operating Time Intent Test), the claimant must intend at acquisition to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA—defined by the CRA as 90% or more) of its operating time throughout its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the claimant's business. As emphasized in Section 3 of the CRA's June 29, 2026 Capital Expenditures Policy, if a claimant intends to use a piece of equipment for SR&ED for only a short period that is less than the property's expected useful life before deploying it into commercial operations, the operating-time intent test is generally not met unless intended SR&ED use across its entire useful life is 90% or more.

Under the alternative second test (the Value Consumption Intent Test), the capital cost of depreciable property qualifies if the claimant intends at acquisition that all or substantially all (90% or more) of the value of the property will be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada. This test is satisfied where rapidly changing technology will render the specialized research asset obsolete and valueless upon conclusion of the R&D project, or where the property will be physically destroyed or structurally degraded during experimental trials; in such cases, the chronological length of the SR&ED project relative to nominal equipment lifespan is irrelevant. To verify acquisition intent during an audit, CRA reviewers examine contemporaneous planning documents—including capital expenditure requests, board authorizations, project plans, business cases, and funding applications—alongside the claimant's historical treatment of similar property in prior years, evaluated within the realistic context of the claimant's overall business operations and contingency plans.

Several strict statutory exclusions govern Line 390 capital expenditure claims. First, non-depreciable assets (such as land), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded from SR&ED eligibility. Second, under the Proxy Method, expenditures for General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) cannot be claimed as capital expenditures. Third, any capital expenditure claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 enters the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance). Fourth, while costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for used equipment (or refurbished used property) meeting the 90% ASA test are entered on Line 390 and included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, used equipment is a prescribed capital expenditure under paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations that does not qualify for SR&ED ITCs and must be deducted on Line 532 of Form T661. Fifth, with respect to computer software (including systems software and licences or rights to use software) incurred after December 15, 2024, software intended to be incorporated into a commercial product is ineligible, whereas software acquired strictly as a tool to perform SR&ED (such as computer-aided design or simulation software) qualifies: if the software benefits only the current fiscal period, it is claimed as a current expenditure; if it is of an enduring nature providing benefits beyond one year, it is claimed as a capital expenditure.
Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) and the Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) Exclusion

New depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test may nevertheless earn SR&ED Investment Tax Credits as Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) under amended subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (revised May 22, 2026) if it is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED carried on in Canada. The SUE calculation is identical under both the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method. Unlike Line 390 ASA property, the capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the full capital cost of SUE under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8, while claiming 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost as a qualified SR&ED expenditure for ITC purposes in each of two consecutive statutory periods.

To qualify as First Term Shared-Use-Equipment, the asset must satisfy six cumulative conditions: it must be depreciable property; it must be acquired after December 15, 2024; it must not meet the 90% ASA test; it must not be General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF); it must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the Income Tax Regulations; it must be new property (never previously used, acquired to be used, or rented for any purpose by any person prior to acquisition by the claimant); and it must actually be used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the "first period," which begins when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 12 months after acquisition. If the claimant's taxation year straddled December 15, 2024 (beginning before December 16, 2024), the SR&ED operating-time percentage must be calculated strictly for the period after December 15, 2024. Property that qualified as First Term SUE subsequently qualifies as Second Term Shared-Use-Equipment if it continues to be actually used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the "second period," which begins when the equipment was acquired and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition. Each qualifying term adds 25% of the capital cost of the equipment (excluding borrowed money costs and deemed capital costs, and reduced by non-arm's-length adjustments under subsection 127(11.6) and related assistance or contract payments) to the claimant's qualified SR&ED expenditures, allowing up to 50% of the capital cost to earn ITCs across both terms.

A critical audit trap in claiming SUE is the Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) anti-avoidance rule under subsection 2900(11) of the Income Tax Regulations. Whereas First Term and Second Term SUE eligibility is evaluated based on actual operating time during the 12-month and 24-month windows, PDP status is evaluated based on the claimant's intended use at the time of acquisition. A property is classified as PDP—rendering it completely ineligible for First Term SUE, Second Term SUE, and ITCs—if at the time of acquisition the claimant intended both: first, to use the property for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a facility, plant, or line for commercial manufacturing, processing, or another commercial purpose; and second, to use the property primarily for non-SR&ED purposes during its operating time over its expected useful life (or to consume its value primarily in non-SR&ED activities).
The CRA's May 22, 2026 Shared-Use-Equipment Policy illustrates this distinction with an explicit manufacturing and processing (M&P) operating-time example:

In this CRA policy scenario, although actual SR&ED usage exceeded 80% during both the First Period (2025) and the Second Period (2026), the claimant installed the new M&P equipment into a commercial production line accounting for over 75% of total plant production and intended at the time of acquisition to use the asset primarily for commercial M&P over its full useful life. Because both PDP conditions were met at acquisition, the equipment is classified as Prescribed Depreciable Property and is completely barred from SUE ITCs. By contrast, the policy confirms that equipment acquired for use in dedicated pilot plants is not considered PDP.
Equipment Lease Costs and Statutory Recapture Rules

For equipment leased after December 15, 2024, lease costs incurred for machinery used all or substantially all (90% or more of operating time) in SR&ED in Canada qualify at 100% under both the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method (excluding GPOEF under the Proxy Method). Where leased equipment is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of operating time) in SR&ED in Canada after December 15, 2024, claimants electing the Proxy Method may claim 50% of the lease costs on Lines 350/355 (and Box 759 of Part 6A), whereas claimants electing the Traditional Method must enter "0" on the primary lease line and instead claim the actual SR&ED-allocated lease costs—including lease costs for equipment used less than 90% of the time—on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures.

When SR&ED capital property or SUE is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, strict statutory recapture rules apply to both the Section 37 expenditure pool and previously claimed ITCs. For 100% ASA capital property previously claimed on Line 390, when the asset is sold, the claimant must report on Line 440 of Form T661 the lesser of the proceeds of disposition and the undeducted SR&ED expenditures for that property remaining in the prior-year pool balance (Line 450), which directly reduces the deductible Section 37 pool. If the proceeds of disposition exceed the undeducted balance on Line 450, the excess—up to the original capital cost minus the Line 440 pool reduction—is included directly in taxable income on Schedule T2SCH1 (Net Income (Loss) for Income Tax Purposes) as recaptured Capital Cost Allowance (CCA). Any proceeds exceeding the original capital cost are taxed as a capital gain or income depending on the facts.

Simultaneously, selling or converting ASA capital property or SUE to commercial use triggers an ITC recapture on T2 Schedule 31 that is added directly to Part I tax payable. For SUE, because only 25% (First Term) or 50% (First and Second Terms combined) of the capital cost qualified for ITCs, only that corresponding percentage of the proceeds of disposition or fair market value is included in the recapture calculation. As illustrated in the CRA's May 22, 2026 Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, if a CCPC acquires new equipment for $160,000 on February 13, 2025 (with a December 31 year-end), claims a 35% First Term SUE ITC in 2025 of $14,000 and a 35% Second Term SUE ITC in 2026 of $14,000 (for a combined ITC of $28,000), and subsequently sells the equipment in 2028 for $100,000, the recaptured ITC is the lesser of $28,000 (total SUE ITCs earned) or $17,500, resulting in a $17,500 addition to Part I tax in 2028.
Unpaid Amounts and Government Assistance Reductions

Under subsection 127(26) of the Income Tax Act and Section 4.1 of the CRA's Total Qualified Expenditure Policy (May 22, 2026), current SR&ED expenditures (other than salaries and wages, which are governed separately by subsection 78(4) on Line 315) that are not paid within 180 days following the end of the taxation year in which they were incurred are deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year for ITC calculation purposes. They are excluded from earning ITCs until the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid. As demonstrated by the CRA's policy example involving "B Limited" (which had a December 31, 2024 year-end and incurred an unpaid $100,000 arm's-length SR&ED contract payable to "C Limited" that was not paid until September 2025, after the 180-day window closed), the claimant must still report the $100,000 contract expenditure on its 2024 Form T661 by the SR&ED reporting deadline to deduct it as an allowable Section 37 expenditure. On the 2024 Form T661, B Limited enters the 20% arm's-length contract reduction ($20,000) and then enters the remaining 80% ($80,000) on the line for "current expenditures (other than salary or wages) not paid within 180 days of the tax year end" (Schedule B, Section 2), excluding 100% of the unpaid invoice from 2024 ITC calculations. When B Limited pays the invoice in September 2025, it enters the $80,000 amount on the line for "payment of prior years' unpaid amounts (other than salary or wages)" on its 2025 Form T661 to include it in 2025 qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes.

Under subsections 127(18) to 127(21) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED at the filing-due date. Direct innovation grants—such as National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) funding—and provincial R&D tax credits reduce qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar. Furthermore, even where a government contribution agreement contains conditional repayment terms—where periodic repayments depend on future commercial revenues from the developed product reaching a specified threshold, subject to a repayment ceiling and a termination date after which unpaid balances are extinguished—the CRA treats the funding as government assistance upon receipt, reducing the Section 37 and Section 127 pools immediately. Only when the claimant makes actual cash repayments of assistance that previously reduced the SR&ED pool can those repayments be added back on Line 454 (Schedule B, Section 1 of Form T661) to restore pool and ITC eligibility in the year of repayment. Where government assistance and contract payments on a project exceed the claimant's SR&ED expenditures on that project, subsections 127(19) and 127(21) require the excess assistance to be allocated across related non-arm's-length parties working on the project using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, revised May 15, 2026), reported on Line 540 of Form T661.
Administrative Governance, 2026 Form Revisions, and Filing Procedures
Canada Revenue Agency Administration and Pre-Claim Approval Process

The Canada Revenue Agency delivers the SR&ED program through four coordinating tax services offices across Canada, deploying a dual-discipline audit teams architecture. Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) evaluate Part 2 of Form T661 to determine whether the claimed activities satisfy subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, while Financial Reviewers audit Part 3 through Part 6 of Form T661 and Schedule 31 to verify payroll allocations, T4 slips, arm's-length and non-arm's-length contracts, post-December 15, 2024 capital asset intent and operating-time logs, and assistance reductions.

To eliminate the historical uncertainty of waiting until after fiscal year-end to learn whether a major R&D initiative qualifies technically, Budget 2025 introduced—and the CRA officially launched on April 1, 2026—the SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval Process. Accessible directly through the CRA's My Business Account (supported by the upgraded SR&ED Client Portal and Self-Assessment and Learning Tool), the Pre-Claim Approval Process enables eligible businesses to submit project protocols prior to starting work or incurring R&D costs and receive a formal determination from the CRA within eight weeks. Securing an upfront technical determination within eight weeks substantially enhances cash-flow predictability and protects claimants against retrospective technical audit disallowances when the T2 corporate tax return is filed.
Prescribed Forms, 2026 Line-Item Updates, and the 18-Month Statutory Deadline

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA published a comprehensive suite of updated prescribed forms and administrative policy manuals across April, May, June, and October 2026 (while Guide T4088, Guide to Form T661, undergoes formal revision supplemented by the CRA's online line-by-line instructions for Form T661(26)). Note that when downloading accessible fillable PDF versions from the CRA website (such as t661-fill-26e.pdf, t2sch31-fill-10-26e.pdf, t2sch49-fill-26e.pdf, and t1145-fill-26e.pdf), claimants must save the file directly to their computer and open it using Adobe Acrobat Reader 10 or later rather than opening it inside a web browser.

body.text: A rigorous audit of a post-Bill C-15 SR&ED filing requires verifying line-by-line accuracy across the newly introduced and reinstated fields on Form T661 (Rev. 26). In Part 2 (Project Information), in addition to the technical narratives describing technological uncertainty, hypotheses, systematic experimentation, and advancements, claimants claiming capital expenditures must enter on Line 262 (and Line 263) the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024 used in each project, including only depreciable property claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 in that taxation year. In Part 3 (Calculation of Allowable and Deductible SR&ED Expenditures), Lines 350 and 355 capture eligible lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED (which must reconcile with Box 759 in Part 6A); Line 360 captures overhead and other expenditures under the Traditional Method (including post-December 15, 2024 lease costs for equipment used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED); Line 390 captures capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 meeting the 90% ASA test (including used equipment for Section 37 pool purposes); Line 440 captures the lesser of proceeds of disposition of SR&ED capital property and the undeducted balance in the prior-year pool on Line 450; and Line 454 (via Schedule B, Section 1) captures repayments of government and non-government assistance that previously reduced the deductible SR&ED pool.

In Part 4 (Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes), Line 532 deducts prescribed capital expenditures (such as used equipment claimed on Line 390) that do not qualify for ITCs; Line 535 reports qualified capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024; Line 540 deducts excess assistance allocated from non-arm's-length parties via Form T1145; Line 543 deducts non-arm's-length cost-markup adjustments under subsections 127(11.6) and 127(11.7) for goods, services, or post-December 15, 2024 depreciable property acquired from NAL suppliers; Lines 508, 538, 544, and 546 track qualified expenditures transferred in or out between NAL parties via Form T1146; and Line 559 computes Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures.

In Part 6 of Form T661 (26), three detailed project and asset breakdowns are now mandatory. Part 6A breaks down project-by-project costs, including salaries (Box 756), Traditional Method overhead and other expenditures (Box 758, corresponding to Line 360), and leased equipment costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (Box 759, which must equal Lines 350/355). Part 6B (Capital Expenditures) requires itemized disclosure of the 20 most expensive capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, reporting the property name (Box 780, matching Line 262 of Part 2), the full capital expenditure amount including purchase price, installation, customs/excise duties, and transportation (Box 782), and the list of associated project numbers (Box 786). Part 6C (Shared-Use-Equipment) requires itemized disclosure of the 20 most expensive SUE properties acquired after December 15, 2024, reporting the SUE property name (Box 788), the purchase date in YYYY-MM-DD format (Box 790), and 25% of the capital cost amount claimed (Box 792). Finally, Part 9 of Form T661 requires mandatory disclosure confirming whether a third-party claim preparer was engaged, detailing the preparer's identification, billing arrangement (contingency percentage versus hourly or flat fee), and total fee; inaccurate or incomplete Part 9 disclosure exposes both the claimant and the claim preparer to joint and several liability for a $1,000 penalty under subsection 162(5.1), alongside third-party civil penalties under Section 163.2.

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file Form T661 containing the prescribed technical and financial information, together with T2 Schedule 31 (or Form T2038(IND)), within 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year under paragraph 150(1)(a), a corporation has a strict 18-month deadline following the end of its fiscal year to file—or to submit an amended Form T661 and Schedule 31 adding forgotten expenditures or projects. As emphasized in corporate tax due-diligence protocols, the Income Tax Act does not permit late-filed Form T661 or Schedule 31 submissions beyond this 18-month statutory bar, nor can the CRA grant ministerial discretion to waive the deadline.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes

Every Canadian province (except Prince Edward Island) and the Yukon Territory provides statutory R&D tax incentives that stack alongside the federal SR&ED program. Because all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, the amount of any provincial credit earned in the taxation year reduces the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool (and the Section 37 deductible pool) before the 15% or 35% federal ITC is calculated.
Ontario R&D Tax Credit Ecosystem (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Since the harmonization of Ontario corporate income tax administration with the federal government after December 31, 2008, Ontario's three statutory R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency through schedules filed with the federal T2 corporate return, piggybacking on the federal Form T661 eligibility determination. To qualify for any of Ontario's three credits, a corporation must maintain a permanent establishment in Ontario and carry out eligible SR&ED work in the province.

First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on T2 Schedule 566, provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit to qualifying corporations on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (100% of direct salaries, 100% of the 55% PPA overhead, 80% of arm's-length contractor payments, and eligible capital expenditures) up to an annual Ontario expenditure limit of $3,000,000, generating a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000. The $3,000,000 Ontario expenditure limit is shared among associated corporations and begins to phase out when the prior-year federal taxable income of the corporation (and associated group) exceeds $500,000, becoming completely eliminated at $800,000 of prior-year taxable income, or as prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada rises from $25,000,000 to $50,000,000.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on T2 Schedule 508, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit to all corporations (both CCPCs and large or foreign-controlled corporations) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures net of any OITC or OBRITC claimed, with no expenditure ceiling. Unused ORDTC may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. Because claiming the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC constitutes government assistance that immediately reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool—thereby reducing a CCPC's 35% cash-refundable federal ITC by 1.225% of total spend in exchange for a non-cash credit that a loss-making startup cannot currently use—the Ontario Taxation Act, 2007 and Section 4.5 of the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy permit a claimant to formally waive (renounce) the ORDTC on Schedule 508 on or before the T2 filing-due date. When the ORDTC is timely renounced, the federal Section 37 and Section 127 pools are not reduced by the 3.5% credit.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on T2 Schedule 568, provides an additional 20% fully refundable tax credit to corporations carrying on business in Ontario for qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred under an eligible research contract with an approved Ontario research institute (such as an Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, or hospital research institute), up to an annual qualified expenditure cap of $20,000,000.
Québec R&D Tax Regime and the 2025–2026 CRIC Consolidation

Unlike Ontario and British Columbia, Québec administers its corporate tax system and R&D tax incentives independently through Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec), with sectoral and institutional recognitions overseen by the Ministère de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie (MEIE). While Québec requires separate provincial tax forms (the RD-222 and RD-1029 series) and conducts independent financial and scientific audits, all Québec R&D tax credits are 100% refundable in cash regardless of whether the claimant is an SME or a large multinational enterprise. However, corporate tax auditors must distinguish between Québec's legacy R&D tax credit system and the sweeping consolidation enacted in the Québec 2025–2026 Budget tabled on March 25, 2025.

For taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Québec operated a multi-credit framework anchored by four primary refundable incentives: the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7), which provided a 30% refundable credit on the first $3,000,000 of eligible Québec R&D salaries (and 50% of Québec subcontractor payments) for SMEs with world assets under $50,000,000 (phasing down linearly to 14% at $75,000,000 in assets) and a 14% refundable credit for large corporations or expenditures exceeding $3,000,000, subject to a per-employee non-eligible exclusion threshold; the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried On by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6, on 80% of eligible contract amounts); the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1, requiring an MEIE validation certificate that carried a $318 plus tax application fee); and the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03).

To streamline administration and align with the federal reinstatement of capital expenditures, the Québec 2025–2026 Budget abolished the separate Tax Credit for Salaries (R&D), the Tax Credit for University Research, the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium, the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, and the industrial design component of the in-house design credit (while retaining the fashion design component) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Transitional provisions allow a taxpayer's eligible consortium fee balance at the end of a taxation year ending after March 25, 2025 to continue generating the consortium R&D tax credit for taxation years ending on or before December 31, 2029, and amend the Act respecting the sectoral parameters of certain fiscal measures so that the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues to issue recognition certificates for eligible public research centres and eligible research consortia.

In place of those abolished credits, Québec enacted the unified, 100% refundable CRIC for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. The CRIC consolidates R&D salaries, subcontractor payments (50% of amounts paid to arm's-length Québec subcontractors and to eligible university entities, public research centres, and research consortia), pre-commercialization activities, and capital expenditures on depreciable property and software used in R&D in Québec into a single regime. Above a simplified single exclusion threshold, the CRIC provides a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures for all corporations regardless of asset size, and a 20% fully refundable credit on all eligible expenditures exceeding $1,000,000.
Western, Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

Across the Western, Prairie, and Atlantic provinces and the Yukon Territory, regional R&D tax credits exhibit distinct rate structures, refundability caps, carryforward horizons, and statutory filing deadlines:

body.text: Cross-provincial tax compliance requires heightened vigilance regarding statutory filing deadlines and regional rate arbitrage. While the federal SR&ED program and provinces such as Ontario, Québec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Newfoundland and Labrador allow 18 months after fiscal year-end to file (for Manitoba and Newfoundland and Labrador, 12 months after the T2 corporate return filing-due date), Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) must be claimed within 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date. The tighter deadlines are the renunciation deadlines: a corporation that wishes to renounce the Manitoba R&D tax credit for federal purposes must do so on or before 6 months after its tax year-end, and written waivers of the Ontario OITC and ORDTC must be filed on or before 6 months after the tax year-end (or on an amended return), well before the 18-month federal reporting deadline. Furthermore, for large or foreign-controlled enterprises that are ineligible for Ontario's OITC or British Columbia's refundable CCPC tier, locating R&D centres in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Manitoba, or Québec unlocks 15% to 30% provincial credits alongside the 15% federal ITC, nearly doubling the combined ~18% non-refundable benefit available in Ontario to ~27.75%–32% with immediate cash refundability on the provincial tier.
Judicial Precedents, Audit Defence, and Contemporaneous Documentation

Canadian SR&ED tax litigation before the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) has established a rigorous body of case law interpreting subsection 248(1) and Section 37 of the Income Tax Act. Mastering these judicial precedents is essential both when structuring project narratives for CRA Research and Technology Advisors and when contesting reassessments before the CRA Appeals Branch or the Tax Court of Canada.
Foundational Appellate Jurisprudence

The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is Justice (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman's landmark decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC). The appellant engineered physical scale hydraulic models—including the White River Diversion Dam—where existing hydrodynamic equations could not reliably resolve complex three-dimensional fluid flow, sediment transport, and ice-jamming uncertainties. Emphasizing that tax incentive legislation encouraging scientific research must be given "such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects", and endorsing Revenue Canada's Information Circular IC 86-4R3 as a generally useful and reliable guide developed through extensive scientific consultation, Justice Bowman articulated the five-criteria judicial test that governs every SR&ED dispute in Canada.

Under Justice Bowman's framework, the court evaluates: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures (noting that if the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering, no technological uncertainty exists); second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty through a five-stage method (observation of the subject matter, identification of the problem, formulation of a hypothesis, testing of the hypothesis by experiment or analysis, and logical conclusions); third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement—an advancement in the general understanding available to competent professionals in the field, even if incremental or resulting in the rejection of a hypothesis; and fifth, whether the taxpayer kept a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed.

Shortly thereafter, the Federal Court of Appeal formally elevated Justice Bowman's five criteria to binding appellate law across Canada in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA, at para. 10) and in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 D.T.C. 6740 (FCA, at para. 17). In RIS-Christie, the Federal Court of Appeal underscored that because scientific research requires verifiability and repeatability of empirical testing, a claimant's failure to produce documentary evidence of test data and experimental results is ordinarily fatal to proving that systematic experimentation occurred. Similarly, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 (affirmed 2011 FCA 355), the courts confirmed that shop-floor modifications to manufacturing machinery executed via intuitive trial-and-error adjustments without formal hypothesis formulation constitute routine engineering rather than SR&ED.

In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (CanLII), Justice Sommerfeldt synthesized two decades of post-Northwest Hydraulic jurisprudence while evaluating claims for custom theatrical winches and acoustic baffling systems. At paragraph 17, Justice Sommerfeldt observed that while there is no single exhaustive statutory definition of "routine engineering," the concept encompasses the application of established engineering principles and predictable techniques by qualified practitioners. At paragraph 26, after reviewing the jurisprudence on Question 2, he defined a "hypothesis" simply as a statement or proposition to be tested by an experiment or a trial. At paragraph 33, he summarized the essential characteristics demonstrating that the scientific method was followed. Most importantly for audit defence, at paragraph 46 (endorsing Justice Jorré's reasoning in 2014 TCC 313 at paragraph 94), Justice Sommerfeldt noted that while contemporaneous documentation is frequently vital to resolving factual disputes between the taxpayer and the CRA, "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific intent, is not a condition" in the statute itself where the taxpayer adduces credible, persuasive evidence proving the five criteria.
Contemporary Tax Court Rulings (2023–2026)

Between 2023 and 2026, a wave of significant decisions from the Tax Court of Canada has refined the evidentiary boundaries of technological uncertainty, failed experimentation, oral testimony, and statute-barred reassessments:
