Food science / commercial frozen pie formulations (2013–2016 claims)

1. Failed Recipes as Advancement: Eliminating unsuccessful formulations after structured analysis of why they failed constitutes a valid technological advancement (rejection of a hypothesis). 2. Oral Testimony: Credible, detailed oral testimony from the CEO (Mr. Pandya) alongside testing records satisfied the 5th Northwest Hydraulic criterion and cured documentary gaps.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159 (amended reasons January 17, 2025)
Beverage preservation / unpasteurized cold-pressed juice & vinegar drink shelf-stability (2020 tax year)
Taxpayer Victory (Appeal allowed; referred back for reassessment)

1. Known Solutions in Novel Contexts: Technological uncertainty exists even where known preservatives exist publicly, provided they have never been used in the specific system context (resolving microbial growth/oxygen release causing exploding cans without pasteurization to achieve 2-year room-temperature stability). 2. Practical Documentation Standard: Contemporaneous records need only track hypotheses, experiments, and results for practitioners in the field; they do not need to be written for an uninitiated outsider to replicate.
Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63
Oilfield engineering / frac water heater development

Reinforces that shop-floor equipment modifications and field trials lacking documented hypothesis formulation, controlled variable isolation, and systematic analytical evaluation fail Questions 2, 3, and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic.
Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173
Industrial heating elements (~$738,000 in SR&ED refunds across multiple years)

Demonstrates that where a claimant makes misrepresentations attributable to neglect, carelessness, or wilful default under ITA subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i), the CRA can reopen statute-barred taxation years 7 to 10 years after initial refunds were paid and claw back the entire SR&ED refund plus interest and penalties.
ExxonMobil Canada Resources Company v. The King, 2026 TCC 42 (March 6, 2026), Docket 2017-5069(IT)G
Resource / Energy engineering (CAD $36,207,810 in pipeline feasibility study costs, 2001 taxation year)
Taxpayer Victory (Appeal allowed; Part XIII assessment vacated)

Held that pre-development feasibility study costs were deductible in computing business income under section 9 of the Act, rejecting the Minister's denial under paragraph 18(1)(a) and the transfer pricing adjustments; the decision concerns general deductibility rather than the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED.

body.text: Two recent taxpayer victories—Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108) and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159)—provide powerful legal ammunition when defending claims against overly restrictive CRA technical reviews. In Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108), the CRA disallowed multiple commercial food-formulation projects conducted between 2013 and 2016, contending that Canafric engaged in routine recipe testing and lacked sufficient written documentation despite on-site CRA review meetings in 2015 and 2018. The Tax Court of Canada overturned the CRA's denial and ruled in favour of the taxpayer. The Court found that Canafric did not simply discard unsuccessful recipes through blind trial and error; rather, its CEO and lead researcher (Mr. Pandya) systematically analysed why each failed recipe did not meet target physical and stability requirements and formulated adjusted hypotheses accordingly. The Tax Court affirmed two vital propositions: first, even where a researcher fails to achieve all commercial targets, the systematic elimination of unsuccessful formulations (the rejection of a hypothesis) constitutes a qualifying technological advancement; and second, documentary evidence is not always strictly mandatory where credible, factually detailed oral testimony from the researcher fills in any gaps in the written record.

In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159, appealing a November 15, 2021 assessment for the 2020 taxation year), the appellant undertook experimental development to control microbial growth and achieve a cold-pressed juice and vinegar-based beverage that was shelf-stable at room temperature for at least two years (the industry benchmark for shelf stability) without thermal pasteurization. During initial experimental trials, microbial growth inside the unpasteurized cold-pressed juice released oxygen and caused the sealed cans to explode. The Minister of National Revenue denied the SR&ED claim on the grounds that the appellant tested preservatives already known to competent food scientists, failed to conduct a systematic investigation, and kept records that could not be replicated by an outsider. Writing for the Tax Court of Canada, Justice Bodie allowed the appeal and established two landmark principles for SR&ED claimants: first, a scientific or technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution or preservative exists, provided it has never been applied in the specific system context and constraints faced by the claimant; and second, contemporaneous documentation is meant simply to keep track of the hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained as the work progressed—it does not need to be designed for someone unfamiliar with the specific field of science or technology to replicate the results.

Conversely, the Tax Court's 2025 decisions in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63)—where an oilfield frac water heater claim was denied due to a lack of documented experimentation—and Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173)—where approximately $738,000 in previously paid SR&ED refunds were reassessed and clawed back seven to ten years later—underscore the severe financial risks of non-compliant claims. Under subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) of the Income Tax Act, if the CRA establishes that a taxpayer made a misrepresentation attributable to neglect, carelessness, or wilful default in an SR&ED filing, the Minister may reopen otherwise statute-barred taxation years indefinitely to claw back refunds. As the CRA explicitly warns in its updated Form T661 (26) instructions, when signing a tax credit application, the claimant remains legally responsible for ensuring a compliant claim even if misled by third-party promotional representations. Furthermore, in litigating SR&ED disputes before the Tax Court of Canada, counsel must also heed BlackBerry Limited v. The King (2023 TCC 137), where Justice Bocock struck out proposed expert reports on the ground of necessity under the R. v. Mohan / White Burgess evidentiary standard, holding that an expert cannot be used merely to interpret or bolster a technical report already before the Court ("the Technical Report is the best evidence of the Technical Report").
Strategic Audit Readiness and Compliance Synthesis

Navigating Canada's post-Bill C-15 SR&ED landscape requires integrating statutory tax planning directly into corporate engineering and capital budgeting workflows. First, for high-value R&D initiatives commencing on or after April 1, 2026, corporate tax directors should utilize the CRA's new Pre-Claim Approval Process via My Business Account prior to starting work or committing capital, securing an upfront eight-week technical eligibility determination from the CRA. Second, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs with substantial balance-sheet equity or debt ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000+ in prior-year taxable capital) should annually model both the taxable capital phase-out formula and the newly available ECPC three-year average gross revenue phase-out election on Schedule 31 and Schedule 49, electing whichever method preserves a larger portion of the doubled $6,000,000 enhanced 35% expenditure limit.

Third, to substantiate reinstated capital expenditures (Line 390 / Part 6B Boxes 780–786) and Shared-Use-Equipment claims (Part 6C Boxes 788–792) for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, claimants must establish rigorous capital governance. Before acquiring research equipment, management should document in contemporaneous capital authorizations and business cases that the property is intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more of operating time or value) in SR&ED across its expected useful life—or, for SUE, that the property is new, is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) intended over its full useful life primarily for commercial manufacturing or processing under subsection 2900(11) of the Regulations, and is tracked via contemporaneous machine-hour logs proving SR&ED operating time across both the 12-month First Period and 24-month Second Period.

Fourth, financial controllers should conduct an annual comparative model between the 55% Proxy Method (Field 160) and the Traditional Method (Field 162)—particularly where post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs are incurred for machinery used less than 90% in SR&ED (claimable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method)—and evaluate whether loss-making Ontario CCPCs should waive the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC on Schedule 508 prior to the T2 filing-due date to prevent government-assistance erosion of the 35% cash-refundable federal ITC. Simultaneously, accounts payable teams must enforce a strict 150-day post-year-end review to ensure all accrued SR&ED bonuses (Line 315) and arm's-length contractor or material invoices (subsection 127(26)) are paid in full before the 180-day statutory cutoff, while executing updated Form T1145 and Form T1146 agreements (revised May 15, 2026) and Line 543 cost-markup eliminations for all non-arm's-length transactions.

Finally, engineering and scientific teams should structure their contemporaneous project repositories—such as Git commits, Jira tickets, experimental test benches, and lab logs—and Part 2 Form T661 narratives explicitly around the five Northwest Hydraulic questions. By clearly distinguishing system-level technological uncertainty from routine engineering in accordance with Joel Theatrical Rigging (2017 TCC 6) and Manning Canning Kitchens (2024 TCC 159), recording quantitative test results, and systematically documenting why failed prototypes or rejected hypotheses advanced the company's technological understanding in accordance with Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108), claimants can withstand rigorous CRA technical and financial audits while meeting the 18-month (Federal, Ontario, Québec, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Newfoundland & Labrador) statutory filing deadlines and the Alberta IEG deadline of 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date.
